Summary: The paper compares LLM generation strategies for drafting OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited (100 entries, 515 papers, 19% readable in full via open access). One model (Claude Opus 5.5) writes, extracts, audits and judges everything under shared guards; only the strategy varies: direct reading of all papers in one prompt, an agentic curator, an evidence graph, case table first, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, three add-ons, and four 'reading better' variants of direct reading. The primary endpoint is coverage of 6,652 atomic facts split once from OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant descriptions (as deposited in ClinVar), credited only in draft text that cites the paragraph's paper. Main results: (1) hiding the full text of the same papers lowers direct reading's coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries; +43.7 points, 45 better/0 worse); (2) at the main settings the agent and the evidence graph are not distinguishable from direct reading (-0.6, -0.5), case table first trails by 1.9 (suggestive), and under matched extraction settings on 38 entries the evidence graph leads by 1.8 (+0.4 to +3.3); (3) a completeness pass adds 2.6 points on 38 held-out entries without lowering audit-judged fidelity, a gain that holds only if the unrevised draft is kept when the revision is stopped; (4) planted-error tests show the claim-level audit catches citation swaps, moved variant sentences and single-value substitutions, but not added citations (a claim takes the best verdict over its cited papers) or omissions. Exploratory runs cover released pipelines (PaperQA2, GraphRAG, STORM), input padding, large entries and 20 entries created in 2026 as a contamination check. No person validated any judgement.
Strengths: The design is clean and controlled. Model, guards, audit and scoring are fixed and only the strategy varies (Sec. 3, Fig. 1, Table 4). A symmetric completion rule plus an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Sec. 3.3, Table 11) keeps the comparison from being confounded by which strategy loses entries.

The within-paper access manipulation is a strong causal design (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a, Table 23): same 46 entries, same 2,120 fixed facts, no arm repaired, +43.7 points (+38.3 to +49.1), 45 better / 0 worse / 1 tied. The effect is large enough that plausible judge error is unlikely to overturn its direction or rough size.

The statistical reporting is careful and appropriately modest. It gives paired bootstrap intervals over entries, better/worse/tied counts with exact sign tests, Holm adjustment for secondary measures (Tables 7-8), and replicate and judge variation (App. E, Table 20) used as a yardstick rather than as the test. It explicitly declines to claim equivalence without a pre-set margin (Sec. 4.2).

The paper is unusually transparent. Every analysis is labelled primary, secondary, post hoc or exploratory (Sec. 3.3, Tables 2-3). Corrected analyses are disclosed, including an earlier 2.1-point evidence-graph deficit that disappeared under symmetric completion (App. M.4). Dropped entries are listed by ID (Tables 5, 28, 54), and design deviations and costs are reported (Apps. J-L, Table 12).

The audit blind-spot analysis is concrete and actionable. Taking the best verdict over cited papers hides over-citation: 0/30 added citations were flagged, although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for 176/176 claims (Table 49, App. L). In real multi-citation paragraphs, 4-7% of (claim, cited paper) pairs are not supporting (Table 52). Anyone building attribution audits should know this.

Memory and contamination are handled seriously: a memory-only control broken down by creation era (Table 16, Fig. 5), 20 compared entries created in 2026 that were not used in development, whose stored drafts are reproduced exactly (App. M.2), and a provenance analysis of conveyed facts (Table 18).

The reading-better prompts were frozen on three training entries before the held-out run (Sec. 4.3, App. I). Fidelity was audited on 20 entries (Table 32), and the dependence of the gain on the fallback rule is reported in the main text (Table 31) rather than hidden.
Weaknesses: No human validated any judgement, which is the main measurement risk for an evaluation paper (Sec. 3.3; Limitation i). The writer's model family does the fact splitting, the present/partly/absent marks, the 'stated' judgements and the audit verdicts. The only stability evidence is self-agreement (95.7%, App. E). The access effect survives this, but the strategy differences (-1.9 to +1.8 points) and the reading-better gains (+1.6 to +3.3) are the same size as a plausible style-correlated judge bias, such as the self-preference the paper itself cites in Sec. 2. Expert labels on a stratified sample, with chance-corrected agreement and per-strategy error rates, are needed before the small-difference claims can be relied on.

For the evidence graph, the claim that 'the order of close designs depends on settings' is confounded with entry composition. On the 38 ablation entries the unmatched evidence graph is already +1.0 against direct reading (Table 22, bottom; App. F). The matched change itself is +0.8 (-0.5 to +2.1; Table 22, top), which cannot be distinguished from zero. In the main run the graph is -1.2 on the 19 ablation entries with half or more full text and +3.1 on the other 19 (App. F), and App. E attributes a sign change between the 30- and 93-entry sets to which entries are averaged. The abstract's 'with settings matched, the evidence graph leads by 1.8 points' therefore mostly reflects the subset. Only the case table's matched gain of +2.1 (+1.1 to +3.2) directly supports dependence on settings.

The primary endpoint rewards recall and has no length or precision counterpart, which matters most for the reading-better results. Mean draft length rises from 10,802 characters (baseline) to 11,837, 14,412 and 14,245 for the checklist, completeness pass and merge (Table 33), roughly in step with their gains (+1.6, +2.6, +3.1). Only about 24% of draft statements have a counterpart in the reference (App. H), so most added content is checked only for fidelity by the audit, not for relevance. Without a length-matched direct-reading control or a reference-precision measure, the gain cannot be attributed to the completeness mechanism rather than to writing more.

The regime and the single model limit the conclusion about strategies. Entries have 2-12 references that fit one prompt, 81% of papers are abstract- or title-only, and a frontier long-context model writes everything; Sec. 5 concedes this regime favours direct reading. The settings that motivate extract-first and agentic designs were attempted but produced no comparable results: 0 of 4 large entries completed (App. K.2), and 10 entries with 30-75 references yielded no findings (App. M.1). The title and abstract ('Strategy or access?') read as more general than the evidence.

Safety-filter stops act as an uncontrolled, strategy-dependent selection mechanism. Completion differs by arm: the completeness arms lose 3 and 6 of 41 entries (Table 28), the agentic curator loses 6 of 30 in 2026 (Table 54), and STORM completes 0 of 10 (App. J). Comparisons then condition on the entries every arm completed. For reading better, counting a lost entry as zero turns +2.4 and +3.1 into -3.5 and -4.8 (Table 31), so the reported gain depends on a fallback rule adopted after the evaluation (Reproducibility statement). No analysis checks whether stopped entries differ in topic, size or access, so selection bias cannot be ruled out.

Several analysis choices were made or changed after results were seen. Fixed fact lists replaced per-draft splitting. The completion rule became symmetric after a first analysis put the graph 2.1 points behind (App. M.4). The matched ablation ran after the main comparison. The stated/not-stated restrictions are post hoc. The claim-selection rule for deleted qualifiers was widened after the run, recovering two flagged items (App. L). The reading-better sensitivity analysis was added after review. Each change is disclosed and several are improvements, but together these forking paths around 1-2 point differences, with the primary endpoint unadjusted across five comparisons (Sec. 3.3), make the small-difference findings exploratory in practice.

The benchmark contribution (contribution 1) is weaker than claimed. The fixed fact lists contain curator wording and are not redistributed (Sec. 3.1 'Reuse'; Ethics statement), so a rebuilt reference must be split again. The stability of a fresh split was not measured, and a different splitting procedure moved levels by 2-5 points (Table 6). Results are comparable only within one split, which limits use as a shared benchmark.

The 'stated in the supplied text' analyses (Fig. 2b-c, Fig. 3, Table 19) rely on a judgement by the same model family that writes the drafts. A fact the model cannot find in the text is plausibly also a fact it fails to convey. Sec. 4.1 acknowledges the contrast holds 'partly by construction', but the headroom estimate (4% of facts not fully conveyed although stated) and the 91.0-94.4% coverage of stated facts inherit this correlation. A manual check of a sample of 'not stated' facts in full-text papers would bound it.

The reference is an indirect proxy for the task. Drafts are phenotype entries, but the primary reference is variant-centred allelic-variant text from OMIM gene entries as deposited in ClinVar, plus HPO annotations (Sec. 3.1). The main text does not say how many of the 515 cited papers have an in-scope curator paragraph, that is, how much of each draft's subject matter the primary endpoint can see. For large entries only 5-10% of references are scored (Table 48).

The released-pipeline comparison (Sec. 4.4, App. J) is too limited for the main-text conclusion. PaperQA2 ran without its agent on 10 entries, GraphRAG on 4 and STORM on none, under a different protocol (six section questions concatenated) and with a substituted 384-dimensional embedder. The -14.5-point PaperQA2 gap mixes design with protocol, as Limitation xi concedes. Either run direct reading through the same six questions or keep this result in the appendix only.

The writing is hard to follow. Most main-text sentences carry several estimates, intervals and caveats, and the paper relies on idiosyncratic terms ('like for like', 'stopped reply', 'reading strategies', 'unrepaired'). Key design facts require cross-referencing appendices: why 91 papers in 49 entries were hidden when 96 papers are readable in full, and that 'held-out' means held out from guide learning and reading-better prompt design but not from development of the main strategies (Limitation viii). The matched rows of Table 1 omit the evidence graph's variant precision and the gene column. The title does not tell an ML reader what the task is.
Questions: Can you add expert labels on a stratified sample covering fact splits, present/partly/absent marks per strategy, stated/not-stated judgements and audit verdicts, and report chance-corrected agreement? In particular, do judge error rates differ between direct-reading and extract-then-write drafts?

Given that graph matched minus graph is +0.8 (-0.5 to +2.1) and the unmatched graph is already +1.0 on the 38 ablation entries (Table 22), how do you separate the effect of settings from entry composition? Would you revise the abstract's 1.8-point statement accordingly?

Can you add a length-matched control for reading better, for example direct reading told to be exhaustive per paper at about 14,000 characters? Alternatively, can you report coverage per character and a precision-like measure, such as the share of draft statements with a reference counterpart, for each arm?
How were the 49 hidden-full-text entries and the 91 hidden papers defined, given that 96 of the 515 papers are readable in full?
How many of the 515 cited papers have at least one in-scope curator paragraph, and what share of each draft's text cites such papers?

Do safety-filter stops cluster by entry characteristics (topic, number or length of papers, access level, creation era)? A bound analysis with best- and worst-case imputation for stopped entries, for the main comparison and the 2026 entries, would show how much the conclusions depend on the completion rule.

Could a second model family, as writer, as judge, or both, be run on a subset such as the 30 replicate entries or the 38 ablation entries? That would test whether the access effect and the ordering of strategies transfer, especially to a smaller-context model.
Would you report a post hoc equivalence test (e.g., TOST at +/-2 points) for the agentic curator and the evidence graph against direct reading, clearly labelled post hoc?
What explains the oldest band's much lower direct-reading coverage (34.9% against 51.2-53.9%; Table 16)? Is it the informativeness of older abstracts, fact granularity or reference structure?

Table 18 shows that of facts conveyed (in full or in part) from abstract-only papers, 34.2% are only partly stated in the paper's own text and 4.1% are in no supplied text, against the 1.7% quoted in Sec. 4.1 for facts conveyed in full. How much of abstract-only coverage comes from inference or recall?
How much do levels and paired differences move under a fresh split by the same procedure? Re-splitting even 50 paragraphs would bound the reuse caveat in Sec. 3.1.
Limitations: The authors' limitations list (Sec. 5, i-xi) is thorough and candid: no human validation, one model family, no comparable results on large sets of papers, an indirect reference, the reference list given to every strategy, open-access text only without supplements, development on the evaluation entries, single runs, and the audit's blind spots.

Not adequately addressed: the recall-type primary endpoint has no length control or precision counterpart, which affects how the reading-better gains and the merge result should be read (Table 33; App. H).
Not adequately addressed: entry composition, not only settings, may explain the evidence graph's lead in the matched ablation (Table 22; App. F); the abstract should reflect this.

Not adequately addressed: safety-filter stops select entries differently per strategy, and the reading-better gain depends on a fallback rule adopted after the evaluation (Table 31; Reproducibility statement).
The benchmark cannot be redistributed and must be re-split by anyone who rebuilds it, with untested split stability, which limits its reuse as a shared benchmark (Sec. 3.1; Ethics statement).

On societal impact, the paper correctly states that generated entries are drafts for expert review, must not be presented as OMIM content, and that a passed audit checks neither correctness nor completeness (Ethics statement). This is appropriate.
